article.headline: 4D Gaussian Splatting Reaches the Browser, No Plugins Required
article.lede: The technology that turns smartphone video into navigable, photorealistic 3D scenes has cleared a significant engineering hurdle: it now runs entirely inside an ordinary web browser. What once demanded CUDA clusters and local GPU installs can render dynamic, time-aware scenes in real time through WebAssembly and WebGL alone.
article.body:
**Gaussian splatting** represents a scene not as polygons but as millions of overlapping 3D Gaussian distributions — translucent ellipsoids, each encoding position, color, and opacity. The renderer composites them to produce images that rival photogrammetry but update far faster than earlier neural approaches like *NeRF* (neural radiance field). The "4D" extension adds a temporal axis: rather than a frozen moment, the model captures how a scene deforms or evolves over time, frame by frame.

The research underpinning the most capable versions of this technique was published at SIGGRAPH 2025. *Splat4D*, from researchers at the University of Hong Kong, Nanyang Technological University, and Google DeepMind, generates high-fidelity 4D content from monocular (single-camera) video using a video diffusion model and an asymmetric U-Net architecture to enforce spatial and temporal coherence. The core problem it solves is real: naive 4D reconstruction from a single moving camera tends to produce flickering artifacts and geometric drift, especially at scene edges.

Running such scenes in a browser without any installation is where the engineering surprise lies. Gauzilla Pro, built by developer Yoshiharu Sato in Rust compiled to *WebAssembly* (WASM), sidesteps the usual CUDA and PyTorch dependencies entirely. WebGL handles rendering; WebGPU powers on-device AI inferencing for tasks like isolating structural geometry. Lock-free multithreading works around WASM's concurrency limitations. The result is photorealistic 3D reconstruction that opens in a tab.

The OCR labels visible in the tweet — "Scene: Fashion, Environment: Street Dome" — suggest a consumer or creative demo, likely a viewer with preset environments. Gauzilla Pro is already in practical use by construction teams for as-built site documentation, where a 4D time-lapse of a build site can be shared with any stakeholder who has a browser. The fashion and retail verticals are an obvious next step, where photorealistic spatial visualization carries clear commercial value.

The convergence of diffusion-enhanced reconstruction (Splat4D) and web-native rendering (Gauzilla) points toward a near future in which **photorealistic digital twins** require neither specialized hardware nor proprietary desktop software. The remaining bottleneck is capture quality and processing time, not the viewer itself.

concepts.definition: A scene-representation technique that models 3D environments as collections of millions of semi-transparent, colored Gaussian ellipsoids rather than polygons. The renderer projects and composites these 'splats' onto a 2D image. It is faster to render at high quality than earlier neural scene representations like NeRF.

An extension of 3D Gaussian splatting that adds time as a fourth dimension, allowing the representation to capture motion and scene changes across frames. Each Gaussian can shift, deform, or change opacity over time, enabling reconstruction of dynamic scenes from video.

A binary instruction format that runs in web browsers at near-native speed. It allows code written in systems languages like Rust or C++ to be compiled once and executed inside any modern browser without plugins. It is increasingly used to bring compute-intensive applications — 3D rendering, physics simulation — to the web.

A newer web graphics API that gives browsers low-level access to GPU hardware, going beyond what the older WebGL standard supports. It enables general-purpose GPU computation (not just graphics) inside the browser, making tasks like AI inferencing or physical simulation feasible without leaving the tab.

An earlier neural scene-representation method that encodes a 3D scene as a continuous function learned by a neural network. It produces photorealistic novel views but is computationally slow to render. Gaussian splatting largely superseded NeRF for real-time applications by replacing the implicit neural function with explicit, rasterizable splats.
